Stocks climbed on Thursday even though the PPI was much hotter than expected.Getty Images

Stocks climbed again on Tuesday, with chipmakers leading the session as they recover from a sharp sell-off from the past weeks.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.03%, while the S&P 500 did so 0.60%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite overperformed, jumping 1.18%. Broadcom, Micron and Advanced Micro Devices were among the names that led the index higher.

Traders will now look at the Federal Reserve's policy decision on Wednesday, when the central bank is expected to leave rates unchanged, offering borrowers a reprieve after September's increase. But with inflation gathering momentum and the economy showing few signs of weakening, another hike could follow before policymakers are ready to declare their work finished.

The expected pause, however, comes ahead of government reports that could strengthen the argument for further tightening. Data scheduled for Thursday are projected to show faster inflation in September and stronger economic growth in the third quarter, supported by consumer spending and business investment tied to artificial intelligence.

Economists expect the annual increase in the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, to reach 3.6%, up from 3.4% in August. Higher gasoline prices linked to the conflicts in the Middle East account for part of that acceleration, but price pressures have also spread to airfares, rents and computers.

That broader increase complicates the Fed's effort to bring inflation back to its 2% target. However, September's unemployment rate stood at 4.2%, while weekly applications for unemployment benefits remained exceptionally low.

The main reason to wait lies in the bond market. After September's rate hike, the yield on the 10-year Treasury climbed toward its highest levels in nearly 25 years, threatening to restrain activity more sharply than officials intended.

Higher Treasury yields can raise financing costs for households and businesses, effectively doing some of the Fed's work. New York Fed President John Williams and Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson subsequently indicated that policymakers could wait for additional evidence before deciding their next move.

But that rationale became less straightforward late last week, when bond yields retreated during a stock selloff driven by concerns about the sustainability of AI demand. An easing in financial conditions could weaken the case for an extended pause.

title: S&P 500 Sell-Off: Is Now the Right Time to Buy the Dip?

S&P 500 Sell-Off: Is Now the Right Time to Buy the Dip?
Ben Gran, The Motley Fool

NVDA

The stock market looks a bit wobbly. After reaching a new record high on Oct. 6, the S&P 500 index (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has declined by about 2.5% since then (as of this writing).

On the one hand, a 2.5% drop in the S&P 500 can be unnerving to some investors. It might be a sign of economic trouble ahead. What if the stock market plunges even further into a 10% correction or a 20% bear market?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

On the other hand, many investors might see a 2.5% price decline in the S&P 500 as a sign that "stocks are on sale" and that it's time to buy more shares of S&P 500 exchange-traded funds (ETFs). This is called "buying the dip" -- investing more money in the stock market when the overall market has "dipped" to lower levels.

Here's the thing: If you can patiently leave your stock portfolio alone for the next several years, asking if it's time to "buy the dip" is the wrong question. For consistent, long-term investors, there is rarely a bad time to invest.

Here's why patient, consistent, "boring" long-term investing is often more lucrative than waiting for the perfect moment to swoop in and "buy the dip."

Image source: Getty Images.
Long-term S&P 500 investing: Rarely a "bad time" to buy

The S&P 500 has delivered average annual returns of 9.98% since 1928. That's a remarkably long-term track record of wealth-building returns despite the massive stock market crashes, global wars, and short-term economic crises along the way. The stock market tends to keep chugging along. Companies make money and pass on some of those earnings to shareholders. Stocks go up.

The past few years for the S&P 500 have been even better than that long-term 98-year average. In the past 10 years, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO) has delivered annualized returns of 15.3%. In the 16 years since the fund's inception, it has delivered annualized returns of 14.94%.

If you just bought shares of VOO and held onto them for five, 10, or 16 years, you would've earned significant returns. Even if you thought you were investing at a "bad time" or the "best time" on any given day.

Time in the market beats "timing the market"

When the S&P 500 is down by a few percent in a month, it's easy to think that "maybe I'll just wait to invest until stocks go down even more. Then I'll buy more shares at a lower price." But this is called market timing, and it doesn't work.

The Single Most Important Metric For Vertiv Stock

At Vertiv (VRT), what matters most is the cash customers pay before delivery on its larger data center projects. Our data does not show that deposit amount on its own, so free cash flow is the closest measure here. Buyers pay a deposit with each order and add more at milestones, a structure management says is driving its cash performance. Even so, the stock lost 38.0% from April 27 to October 26, 2026, while the S&P 500 gained 7.6%. Deposits kept rolling in during the June quarter. But the stock was higher on June 30 than on April 27, so the fall came after that quarter, starting with a 17.3% drop on July 29. So how much cash is Vertiv bringing in?

Vertiv's Quarterly Free Cash Flow Has More Than Tripled

So far, customers are paying ahead. Vertiv reported free cash flow of $925 million in fiscal Q2 2026, the quarter ended June 30, up from $277 million a year earlier. On the July 29 call, management said the quarter's rise in deferred revenue came from project advance payments and milestone collections. They added that those deposits were behind the company's working capital and cash performance.

Over the twelve months to June 30, 2026, Vertiv's free cash flow came to 25.5% of revenue. That compares with 18.6% at Emerson Electric, the highest of the three peers Trefis tracks for the company. So Vertiv turns more of each dollar of sales into cash than any of those peers, though part of that cash is deposits customers paid ahead of the sales.

Are The Delays Vertiv Reported In July Only Timing?

So far, management says they are. On the July 29 call, management described minor timing shifts in second-quarter revenue, mainly from multiphase project execution and temporary supply chain dynamics. Revenue still reached $3.27 billion, up 24.1% from a year earlier. That growth was slower than in fiscal Q1 2026, when it was 30.1%.

Management also raised its full-year outlook and now expects 2026 net sales of $14 billion at the midpoint, up 37% from 2025. Asked on the call whether the delays would recur, management said Vertiv was still on a learning curve and had been prudent in its second-half outlook. Yet revenue in both quarters so far grew more slowly than the 37% the full-year outlook calls for, so the second half has to grow faster.

The deposits do not answer this worry. Upfront cash does not get a project delivered any faster, and management would not give the exact amount of revenue the delays pushed out. For now, the view that the delays are only timing is management's own, backed by a raised outlook rather than by a reported result.

U.S. Bancorp (USB): buy, sell, or hold post Q3 earnings?

U.S. Bancorp has followed the market's trajectory closely, rising in tandem with the S&P 500 over the past six months. The stock has climbed by 6.8% to $59.79 per share while the index has gained 6.3%.

Is now the time to buy U.S. Bancorp, or should you be careful about including it in your portfolio? Get the full stock story straight from our expert analysts, it's free.

Why is U.S. Bancorp not exciting?

We're cautious about U.S. Bancorp. Here are three reasons why there are better opportunities than USB, plus one stock we'd rather own.

1. Net interest income points to soft demand

Our experience and research show the market cares primarily about a bank's net interest income growth as one-time fees are considered a lower-quality and non-recurring revenue source.

U.S. Bancorp's net interest income has grown at a 6.8% annualized rate over the last five years, worse than the broader banking industry and in line with its total revenue. Its growth was driven by both an increase in its outstanding loans and net interest margin, which represents how much a bank earns in relation to its outstanding loan book.

U.S. Bancorp trailing 12-month net interest income
2. Low net interest margin reveals weak loan book profitability

The net interest margin (NIM) is a key profitability indicator that measures the difference between what a bank earns on its loans and what it pays on its deposits. This metric measures how efficiently it can generate income from its core lending activities.

Over the past two years, we can see that U.S. Bancorp's net interest margin averaged a weak 2.8%, indicating the company has weak loan book economics.

U.S. Bancorp trailing 12-month net interest margin
3. EPS growth has stalled

We track the long-term change in earnings per share (EPS) because it highlights whether a company's growth is profitable.

U.S. Bancorp's flat EPS over the last five years was below its 6% annualized revenue growth. This tells us the company became less profitable on a per-share basis as it expanded.

U.S. Bancorp trailing 12-month EPS (non-GAAP)
Final judgment

U.S. Bancorp isn't a terrible business, but it doesn't pass our bar. That said, the stock currently trades at 1.5× forward P/B (or $59.79 per share). Investors with a higher risk tolerance might like the company, but we think the potential downside is too great. We're pretty confident there are superior stocks to buy right now. We'd recommend looking at one of our all-time favorite software stocks.
